scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): a two-view response that leans toward saving species while taking the cost view seriously; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose at about 400 words on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: The question of how far we should go to save endangered species has no easy answer.
Some people believe society should try to save every species whatever the cost, while others believe we should not make extraordinary efforts when money and jobs are at stake.
I find more truth in the first view, but I believe our efforts to save species must still be balanced against real human needs.

sections.role: Body 1 — Why I lean toward saving species

sentences.text: First, the view that we should work hard to save species rests on strong reasons.
Each species forms part of a delicate web of life that ultimately supports human survival.
For example, losing the insects that pollinate our crops could damage the food supply of millions.
This shows that protecting species often means protecting ourselves as well.
Many medicines and materials, moreover, have come from plants and animals we nearly lost.
There is also a moral case against wiping out other living things for our own convenience.
For these reasons, I largely share the belief that species are worth real effort to save.

sections.role: Body 2 — Taking the cost view seriously

sentences.text: Second, however, the opposing view rightly reminds us that such efforts carry heavy costs.
Saving certain species can cost enormous sums and threaten the jobs of ordinary workers.
Consider a town whose livelihood disappears when an industry is shut down to protect one rare animal.
Such hardship shows that conservation cannot ignore the real suffering it may cause people.
Public money spent on every species is money not spent on hospitals, schools, or the poor.
A wise policy must therefore weigh the value of a species against the human cost of saving it.
Both views, then, capture part of the truth and must be brought together.
In conclusion, I lean toward the belief that society should work hard to save endangered species.
But the opposing view is right that we cannot ignore the cost in money and jobs.
The wisest course is to protect species seriously while weighing each effort against genuine human needs.
